name: Mozambique
card_headline: Insurgents spread south and west in Cabo Delgado while TotalEnergies restarts its gas project, and opposition leader Mondlane goes on trial for terrorism incitement.
card_summary: Islamic State Mozambique fighters still operate across northern Cabo Delgado and have moved south, west and toward Niassa. Rwandan troops guard the gas zone, and TotalEnergies restarted construction on 29 January. Opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane went on trial on 17 November on five charges tied to the 2024 post-election protests, in which Amnesty cites civil society counts of more than 300 dead. About 1.8 million people need aid, and the 2026 humanitarian plan was 43 percent funded in August. Public debt is about 91 percent of GDP.
card_local: Club of Mozambique, relaying Lusa, reports the Mondlane trial opened on 17 November with a 44-page indictment and a 223-page defence challenge. [1] Zitamar News co-published the June press-freedom investigation. [2] Mediafax and @Verdade were not read directly.
card_international: Al Jazeera and AP report the five charges against Mondlane, and Reuters reported the 29 January LNG relaunch with a 2029 first-LNG target. [3][4][5]
card_scholar: ACLED finds Islamic State Mozambique dispersing south and west while holding a coastal base, and ISS questions how Rwanda's deployment will be paid for. [6][7]
context_md: The insurgency in Cabo Delgado began in October 2017, and ACLED counts at least 6,632 deaths since. [8] Mozambique LNG was suspended in March 2021 after attacks and resumed in January 2026. [9] Crisis Group wrote in 2022 that Rwandan and SADC troops had weakened the insurgency without defeating it, and recommended political dialogue. [10] In the October 2024 election the Constitutional Council gave Frelimo's Daniel Chapo 65.17 percent and Venâncio Mondlane 24.19 percent, and Mondlane rejected the result. [11] Protests followed, and Amnesty cites civil society counts of more than 300 deaths. [12] Chapo was sworn in in January 2025. [11]

sections.title: Cabo Delgado: fighters disperse and move south and west, and the UN says no military victory is near
sections.body_md:
ACLED counts at least 6,632 deaths from political violence in Cabo Delgado since 1 October 2017, 2,772 of them civilians, as of mid-June 2026. [8] The UN humanitarian office OCHA recorded more than 400 conflict incidents in the first half of 2026, 10 percent more than a year earlier. [13]

ACLED's 2026 updates describe fighters dispersing across the province. Its August update says state forces and Rwandan troops are pressing Islamic State Mozambique (ISM) in the Catupa forest in Macomia district, and that ISM has spread south and west, threatening roads and mining sites. Miners were kidnapped at the Muaja gold mines in Ancuabe district on 20 July. On 26 July ISM held at least 10 people for ransom on the R698 in Montepuez district, and on 31 July a group of up to 150 fighters moved north toward Niassa. [6] In November 2025 ACLED recorded the highest monthly fatality rate of the insurgency, with more than 60,000 people fleeing from Eráti and Memba districts in Nampula. [14]

ACLED's Peter Bofin wrote in June that ISM is building an enclave along more than 100 km of the coast and about 50 km inland, with fewer civilian killings there since 2022 and more preaching, roadblocks and coercion. [15] President Daniel Chapo told a 3 February ceremony that the security forces, backed by Rwandan troops and Tanzanian forces at the border, had made significant advances and that displaced people were returning. The state news agency AIM carried the speech without independent checks. [16] UN Special Rapporteur Ben Saul, after a visit from 4 to 14 August, said attacks on civilians had grown in frequency, severity and scale over the past year and that military victory does not look imminent. [17] IOM counted 1,235 people fleeing attacks in Mocímboa da Praia, Macomia, Muidumbe and Meluco between 14 and 27 October. [18]

lenses.local: Club of Mozambique relays the OCHA count of more than 400 incidents in six months, and the state news agency AIM reports the president's claim of significant advances. [13][16]
lenses.international: Africanews reports the UN rapporteur's finding that attacks on civilians have grown and that military victory is not in sight. [17]
lenses.scholar: ACLED finds ISM spreading south and west while keeping a coastal base, and Bofin argues that military means alone will struggle to undo its coastal strategy. [6][15]

sections.title: Rwanda's troops hold the north, and who pays for them is open
sections.body_md:
Rwanda's forces are the main security presence around the gas zone. ISS researcher Borges Nhamirre put the Rwandan deployment at about 5,000 troops in March, roughly 3,000 of them guarding the LNG project and the towns of Palma and Mocímboa da Praia, under a status of forces agreement that runs until at least 2029. [9] Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo said on 2 April that personnel exceed 6,300, up from about 2,000 in 2021, and called some media reports on troop numbers inaccurate. [19]

Money is the open question. Senior Rwandan officials threatened on 14 March to withdraw unless sustainable international funding is found, during Chapo's visit to Brussels, and reports said the EU would not renew its funding after May. ISS authors put EU money since 2022 at about $46 million, roughly 17 percent of Rwanda's reported deployment costs. [7] Makolo said Rwanda has not sought and will not seek more money from the European Peace Facility, and that funding is a matter for Mozambique and the partners with investments in the province. [19] The ISS authors read the threat as possible pressure on Washington and Brussels and say the warning may not be genuine. [7] This draft did not confirm from an opened source whether the EU decision was formally taken.

ACLED's August update says the Northern Operational Theatre command moved to Mocímboa da Praia, where the Rwandan headquarters is based, and that Rwandan troops helped retake Namabo on 28 June. [6] The UN rapporteur said Rwandan support has produced an offensive defence posture that dampens hostilities but risks letting the group rebuild. [17]

lenses.international: The Rwandan government's own statement and the UN rapporteur's report are the main public accounts opened for this draft. [19][17]
lenses.scholar: ISS says Mozambique's forces cannot secure the territory alone, that the EU faces a dilemma over funding a force whose government is accused of a role in the DRC conflict, and that Rwanda's warning may be a pressure tactic. [7]

sections.title: The gas restart: construction resumed in January, a cost dispute of about $2 billion remains, and Exxon is next
sections.body_md:
TotalEnergies and the government relaunched the roughly $20 billion Mozambique LNG project at a ceremony in Afungi on 29 January 2026. Construction had been halted in 2021. Reuters reported capacity of 13 million tonnes a year, a first LNG target of 2029, and Rwandan soldiers deployed around the site. TotalEnergies holds 26.5 percent, Mitsui 20 percent and the state company ENH 15 percent. [5] ISS's Nhamirre notes that up to 17,000 workers sit inside a securitised enclave that limits supply contracts for local businesses, and that the project's benefits for Cabo Delgado are far from guaranteed. [9]

Costs are contested. TotalEnergies wrote to the government in October 2025 saying costs rose by $4.5 billion during the hold and asked for a 10-year extension. [5] The government granted 4.5 years and ordered an audit. [14] ACLED's June update says Mozambique is resisting roughly $2 billion of the claim. [8] An Oilprice report citing an anonymous source speaking to Bloomberg says a Bayphase audit could not confirm TotalEnergies' claimed costs and that the updated development plan is not yet approved. [20] That rests on one anonymous source.

On 17 November the Council of Ministers approved ExxonMobil's amended Rovuma LNG plan. Onshore capacity rises to 18.6 million tonnes a year from 15.2 million approved in 2019, Standard Bank estimates a cost near $30 billion, and Exxon expects a final investment decision by the end of 2026. [21] World Oil reported a startup target of 2031 in August. [22] A Club of Mozambique headline on 16 November says Eni expects a final investment decision on an FLNG expansion by 2027. [23]

HRW reports that Mozambican prosecutors opened an investigation in March 2025 into alleged 2021 abuses by security forces guarding the TotalEnergies project, and that TotalEnergies denied knowledge of them. [24] ACLED notes a criminal complaint filed in France on 17 November 2025 accusing TotalEnergies of complicity in alleged abuses linked to a 2021 incident at its site. [14]

lenses.local: Club of Mozambique carried the government's November 2025 statement that the audit had no deadline and that TotalEnergies could resume once it submitted a schedule within 30 days. [25]
lenses.international: Reuters reported the January relaunch and the open cost talks, and Oilprice, citing Bloomberg, reports the Bayphase finding. [5][20]
lenses.scholar: ISS says the project resumed before the audit concluded or was published, and warns that the enclave could feed local resentment that insurgents might use for recruitment. [9]

sections.title: The Mondlane trial: five charges, a 223-page defence challenge and a contested immunity ruling
sections.body_md:
Venâncio Mondlane, leader of the Anamola party and runner-up in the October 2024 presidential election, went on trial at the Supreme Court in Maputo on 17 November 2026. Al Jazeera, citing AFP and AP, reports five charges, the gravest being instigation of terrorism, which carries up to 24 years. He denies them. [3] At the first hearing the Public Prosecutor's Office read a 44-page indictment of 107 points, presented by Deputy Attorney-General Amabélia Chuquela. It argues that his calls for strikes and marches, made in videos from October to December 2024, are linked to violence and damage. The road concessionaire Revimo is an assisting party and says it lost toll revenue. The defence announced a 223-page written challenge, and Judge Luís Mondlane suspended the session about an hour early, saying lawyers should have filed it in advance. [1] AP says Mondlane argued the Attorney General's Office held the accusation for 130 days and asked that it be declared null. [4]

Mondlane sits on the Council of State, which suspended his immunity on 10 June. The decision became public in late August, and he calls it null because he says the Council lacks the power. [26] The Constitutional Council gave Daniel Chapo 65.17 percent and Mondlane 24.19 percent in 2024, and Mondlane rejected the result. [11] ISS wrote that observers reported widespread irregularities. [27]

The death toll is disputed. Amnesty says civil society counted more than 300 deaths and over 3,000 injuries in the crackdown, while police put protest deaths at 96, including 17 officers. The Attorney General announced 651 cases in February 2025 and has released no further details. [12] AP cites civil society groups for at least 400 killed. [4] Mondlane said in April that 55 Anamola supporters had been killed and 436 cases of grave violence recorded, figures with no independent verification in the report carrying them. [28] International IDEA's tracker says the commission running the national dialogue opened public hearings in June, with civil society warning that public trust in the process is fragile. [29]

lenses.local: Club of Mozambique, relaying Lusa, reports the indictment, the defence challenge and the judge's rebuke in detail. [1]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and AP both report the charges but differ on the toll, with Amnesty cited for more than 300 dead and civil society groups for at least 400. [3][4]
lenses.scholar: Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera in September described the case as a judicialisation of politics and said a conviction could bar Mondlane from the 2029 race, a point ISS made in 2025. [11]

sections.title: Journalists and critics: an abducted editor, seized equipment and a reporting blackout in the north
sections.body_md:
Forbidden Stories and nine partner outlets, including Zitamar News, published the Mozambique Exposed investigation on 9 June 2026, drawing on nearly 100 interviews. It says authorities are trying to impose a media blackout on the Cabo Delgado conflict and that local journalists who try to cover it are targeted. Mozambican authorities did not respond to its questions. [30] Zitamar News published the reports on 9 and 10 June. [2]

The named cases are specific. Arlindo Chissale, a Pinnacle News reporter, was abducted on 7 January 2025 on the road between Pemba and Nacala and has not been seen since. [30] His family told Carta in January 2025 that he was missing. [31] HRW says his family later confirmed his torture and death, though his body had not been recovered by October 2025. [24] Ibraimo Mbaruco of Palma Community Radio has been missing since 7 April 2020, and the Attorney General's Office closed the case for lack of evidence in August 2024. [31] Blogger Albino Sibia was shot dead by police in December 2024 while livestreaming a protest. [30]

Estacio Valoi, editor of Moz24h, was declared a formal suspect on 23 April 2026 after a criminal defamation complaint by Safi Timber. On 16 June three agents of the criminal investigation service SERNIC seized his phones, computers and tablets at his home in Pemba. CPJ called for the equipment to be returned. [32] HRW reports that soldiers detained and questioned 16 journalists in Macomia in June 2025 and seized their equipment, and that unidentified gunmen shot dead at least 10 opposition officials between October 2024 and March 2025 without credible investigation. [24] ACLED reports that Catholic Bishop Osório Citora Afonso was shot dead in Quelimane on 6 June 2026 and that three people have been arrested. [8] Joseph Hanlon's newsletter says five journalists have been killed since the 2023 elections but names only Chissale, so that count is unverified. [33]

lenses.local: Zitamar News co-published the June investigation, and Carta's reporting on Chissale reached readers through Club of Mozambique. [2][31]
lenses.international: CPJ and Forbidden Stories document the Valoi prosecution and the blackout, and HRW's annual report records the detentions of journalists in Macomia. [32][30][24]
lenses.scholar: Hanlon's newsletter summarises the Forbidden Stories findings and cites HRW on the absence of credible investigations into the killings of critics. [33]

sections.title: 1.8 million people need aid, the plan was 43 percent funded in August, and floods and El Niño add pressure
sections.body_md:
UNICEF's situation report for July, issued on 18 September, says 1.8 million people need humanitarian assistance, 1 million of them children. It counts 506,214 conflict-displaced people and 715,101 returnees, and 28,163 people displaced by conflict since January, 65 percent of them women and children. It reports a 49 percent gap on a $58.8 million appeal. [34] IOM's September round counted 363,606 displaced people in 213 sites, 205,921 of them in Cabo Delgado and 95,385 in Sofala. The IOM and UNICEF counts use different scopes and are not reconciled in the sources opened here. [35]

OCHA's Cost of Inaction report, as relayed by Club of Mozambique, says the 2026 humanitarian plan needs $534 million and was 43 percent funded in August. It says conflict is spreading into districts with little prior exposure and that abduction is increasingly used for ransom and forced recruitment, including of children. Floods affected more than 724,000 people, and cholera has caused more than 9,500 cases and 89 deaths since September 2025. In some of the most food-insecure districts, food aid has dropped to once every two months, covering 39 percent of minimum caloric needs. [13]

A ReliefWeb key message update reports Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity in conflict-hit Cabo Delgado and northern Nampula and in flood and drought-hit southern and central areas. It warns that without funding, Cabo Delgado food beneficiaries could fall from 420,000 to 265,000. [36] UNICEF cites FEWS NET projecting Crisis-level food insecurity in the south and centre from October 2026 to January 2027, with El Niño expected to peak toward the end of 2026 and the largest impacts in Maputo, Gaza and Inhambane. [34]

lenses.local: Club of Mozambique relays OCHA's funding, flood and cholera figures. [13]
lenses.international: RTP, using Lusa copy, reports the IOM displacement counts by province. [35]

sections.title: Debt near 91 percent of GDP, growth of 0.5 percent, and a new IMF programme expected by year end
sections.body_md:
The IMF Executive Board's 2025 Article IV conclusion, dated 17 February 2026, estimates growth of 0.5 percent in 2025, down from 2.1 percent in 2024, public debt at 91.4 percent of GDP and a total fiscal deficit of 4.5 percent of GDP. It puts inflation at 3.2 percent at the end of 2025. Directors welcomed the planned LNG resumption and Mozambique's removal from the FATF grey list, and flagged high debt, weak growth, security challenges and climate shocks. [37]

After a staff visit in June, the IMF said the government has asked for a fund-supported arrangement and that fiscal and debt vulnerabilities persist. [38] AIM reported on 11 September that the Finance Ministry hopes to reach a staff-level agreement and board approval by the end of 2026, that the government repaid its IMF debt early in March (about 515 million SDR, roughly $630 million), and that Finance Minister Carla Loveira said the treasury still manages liquidity challenges. AIM is state-run, so these are the government's own statements. [39]

Gas revenue is the government's expectation. Reuters cited a figure of up to $35 billion for the state over the life of Mozambique LNG. [5] Oilprice reports that the state could receive about $121 billion over the 25-year life of Rovuma LNG and that 25 percent of the gas is reserved for the domestic market. [21] ISS says gas revenue and contracts need transparent management. [9]

lenses.local: AIM, the state agency, reports the Finance Ministry's timetable for an IMF agreement and the early repayment of IMF debt. [39]
lenses.international: Reuters and Oilprice report the state's projected gas revenues, and the IMF's own releases carry the debt and growth figures. [5][21][37]
lenses.scholar: ISS warns that the economic benefits of the LNG restart for Cabo Delgado are far from guaranteed and urges transparent revenue management. [9]

timeline.text: The Cabo Delgado insurgency begins; ACLED counts deaths from 1 October 2017.
Mozambique LNG is suspended after insurgent attacks.
Chapo is declared winner of the presidential election with 65.17 percent; Mondlane rejects the result and protests follow.
Mondlane's lawyer Elvino Dias and Podemos spokesperson Paulo Guambe are shot dead in Maputo.
Pinnacle News reporter Arlindo Chissale is abducted between Pemba and Nacala.
Chapo and Mondlane meet in Maputo for the first time since the election.
Prosecutors file five charges against Mondlane.
The government grants TotalEnergies a 4.5-year extension and orders an audit; ISM's attacks in Nampula reach a record monthly fatality rate.
TotalEnergies and the government restart construction of Mozambique LNG at Afungi.
Senior Rwandan officials threaten to withdraw troops unless funding is found.
Catholic Bishop Osório Citora Afonso is shot dead in Quelimane.
Forbidden Stories and partners including Zitamar News publish Mozambique Exposed.
The Council of State suspends Mondlane's immunity.
SERNIC agents seize journalist Estacio Valoi's phones and computers in Pemba.
UN Special Rapporteur Ben Saul reports that attacks on civilians have grown and that military victory is not imminent.
An IMF mission begins talks on a possible Extended Credit Facility programme.
IOM reports 363,606 displaced people in 213 sites.
IOM reports 1,235 people fled attacks in four Cabo Delgado districts between 14 and 27 October.
Mondlane's trial opens at the Supreme Court; the Council of Ministers approves ExxonMobil's amended Rovuma LNG plan.

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters and AP file on the LNG restart and the Mondlane trial, but sustained attention is episodic. [5][4] ACLED runs a dedicated Mozambique monitor with Zitamar News, and Forbidden Stories described efforts to restrict reporting from the north. [15][30]

severity.basis: ACLED counts at least 6,632 deaths since 2017, OCHA counted more than 400 incidents in the first half of 2026, up 10 percent, and ISM has moved into new districts. [8][13][6]
1.8 million people need aid, the 2026 plan was 43 percent funded in August, and floods affected more than 724,000 people. [34][13]

Mondlane is on trial on terrorism-related charges, Amnesty cites more than 300 deaths in the 2024 to 2025 crackdown with no published outcome from the 651 cases opened, and journalists have been abducted. [3][12][30]
Growth was 0.5 percent in 2025, public debt is 91.4 percent of GDP, and the government has asked the IMF for a programme. [37][38]
Incidents rose 10 percent and fighters entered new districts, while the LNG restart, a dialogue commission and the IMF request point the other way. [13][6][5][29][38]

parts.basis: France's TotalEnergies leads the $20 billion Mozambique LNG project, ExxonMobil's Rovuma LNG is nearing a final investment decision, and Rwanda, the EU and Russia's foreign minister have each engaged on security. [5][21][7][6]
Mozambique LNG is planned at 13 million tonnes a year and Rovuma at 18.6 million, with Rovuma output possibly in the early 2030s. [5][21]
ISM groups have crossed into Nampula and moved toward Niassa, and Tanzanian forces guard the border. [6][16]
About 1.5 million people have been displaced by the conflict and 1.7 million need aid in 2026. [17]
A European Union fund has paid part of a foreign force's costs, a French complaint accuses TotalEnergies of complicity in abuses, and the UN rapporteur reviewed counter-terrorism law. [7][14][17]

summary: Mozambique matters beyond its borders mainly through future gas supply and through the question of who pays a foreign force to protect an energy project. [9][7] Its trade weight today is small, and the score reflects planned capacity more than current output. [5][21]
gi.up: A successful attack on the Afungi site, a Rwandan withdrawal or a final investment decision that brings Rovuma output closer would raise it.
gi.down: A settled funding arrangement for the Rwandan force and a sustained fall in ISM activity would lower it.

gaps: Local outlets: Carta de Mocambique, @Verdade, Mediafax and Pinnacle News could not be opened directly in this session. Carta appears only through one Club of Mozambique republication from January 2025, and Pinnacle News only through CPJ and Forbidden Stories. Local sourcing leans on Club of Mozambique, Zitamar News listings and state agency AIM.
Radio Mocambique and TVM were not read. AIM, the state news agency, is cited three times and is flagged state_affiliated; Al Jazeera is flagged as state-funded.
Chatham House: only 2020 and 2021 pieces surfaced in search and none was opened. The Crisis Group source is from February 2022 and no 2026 Crisis Group report was found.
Whether EU funding for the Rwandan deployment formally ended in May 2026 was not confirmed from an opened source; the Bloomberg report was not opened.
Rwandan troop numbers conflict (ISS about 5,000, ISS over 4,000 elsewhere, Rwandan government more than 6,300) and no independent count was found.
Displacement counts differ by scope: UNICEF cites 506,214 conflict-displaced people and IOM counted 363,606 displaced in sites. The figures are not reconciled here.
The post-election death toll is disputed: police say 96, Amnesty cites civil society at more than 300, AP cites civil society at least 400.
Mondlane's claim of 55 supporters killed and 436 grave violence cases rests on his own statements relayed by Lusa and has no independent check.
The Oilprice report on the Bayphase audit rests on an anonymous Bloomberg source and carries no publication date. The audit itself has not been published in the sources read.
ACLED's latest update opened is from August 2026; September to November 2026 updates were not found, so the cumulative fatality figure is as of 14 June 2026.
The Mondlane trial schedule after 18 November was not retrieved, and the court's refusal of a live broadcast was seen only in headlines.
Hanlon's count of five journalists killed since the 2023 elections names only one person and is unverified.
Only two books were verified through pages opened; a third was not located, so the books list is short.
Podcast and film items are dated (2021 to 2024) and link to listing or hosting pages; the Global Initiative episode shows no date or length.
Several pages were read through summaries of the page text and not in full, including the Reuters relaunch article, the IMF releases and the OCHA report relayed by Club of Mozambique.

change_reason: v2: long-form issue sections, private-sector coverage, podcasts, media, fact-checks

reporters.name: Luis Nhachote
reporters.bio: Wrote the 8 September 2026 Al Jazeera analysis of the Mondlane trial, reporting from Maputo.
reporters.why: The piece sets out the five charges, the June suspension of immunity and the views of a veteran journalist, a lawyer and a Maputo researcher.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Borges Nhamirre
reporters.role: Researcher on transnational threats and organised crime, ISS
reporters.bio: Wrote the ISS Today analyses of the Chapo and Mondlane meeting (27 March 2025) and of the LNG restart (2 March 2026).
reporters.why: He ties the gas restart to troop numbers, contract secrecy and local grievances, with dates and figures.
reporters.label: ISS Today

reporters.name: Peter Bofin
reporters.bio: Author of ACLED's 26 June 2026 report on Islamic State Mozambique's coastal enclave, produced with Zitamar News.
reporters.why: His report is the most detailed recent account of how the insurgents deal with communities on the coast.
reporters.label: ACLED

reporters.name: Joseph Hanlon
reporters.role: Editor, Mozambique News Reports and Clippings
reporters.bio: Edits a self-funded newsletter distributed through the JISC dev-mozambique list and hosted by the Open University.
reporters.why: Issue 670 (10 June 2026) summarises the Forbidden Stories findings on killed and abducted critics and journalists.
reporters.label: Open University

reporters.name: Estacio Valoi
reporters.bio: Reports on natural resources, including timber smuggling and the Quirimbas National Park; CPJ documents his 2026 prosecution and the seizure of his devices.
reporters.why: His case shows how reporting on resources in Cabo Delgado is met with legal and police pressure.
reporters.label: Committee to Protect Journalists

reporters.name: Alexander Abdelilah and Mariana Abreu
reporters.bio: Bylined the 9 June 2026 Forbidden Stories article on the media blackout in Cabo Delgado, part of Mozambique Exposed.
reporters.why: The investigation drew on nearly 100 interviews and 30 journalists, with Zitamar News among the partners.
reporters.label: Forbidden Stories

reporters.name: Eric Morier-Genoud
reporters.bio: Author of Towards Jihad? Muslims and Politics in Postcolonial Mozambique.
reporters.why: Religion Unplugged reports his finding that the insurgents grew from one small sect, not from mainstream Muslim groups.
reporters.label: Religion Unplugged

reporters.name: Adriano Nuvunga
reporters.bio: Guest on the Africa Daily episode of 7 March 2024 on peace in Cabo Delgado.
reporters.why: A Maputo-based voice on the conflict and on governance who also appears on the Global Initiative's Deep Dive episode.
reporters.label: Africa Daily

books.title: Towards Jihad? Muslims and Politics in Postcolonial Mozambique
books.author: Eric Morier-Genoud
books.why: Reviewer Jacob Judah says it traces relations between Frelimo and Muslims and the origins of the Cabo Delgado insurgency, and that its Cabo Delgado material is brief.
books.label: Engelsberg Ideas (review, 4 December 2023)

books.title: Mozambique's Cabo Delgado Conflict: International Humanitarian Law and Regional Security
books.author: Marko Svicevic and Martha M. Bradley (eds)
books.why: A multidisciplinary African-perspective analysis of the conflict since 2017, covering humanitarian law, regional security and terrorism.
books.label: Routledge

podcasts.title: What will it take for Mozambique's Cabo Delgado to find peace?
podcasts.guest: Adriano Nuvunga, Center for Democracy and Human Rights
podcasts.why: Short background on the insurgency's causes and displacement. Dated, so use it for context and not for current figures.

podcasts.title: The Insurrection in Mozambique's Cabo Delgado
podcasts.why: Crisis Group's analyst on who the insurgents are and the turn to Rwanda in 2021. Old, but it explains how the foreign deployments began.

podcasts.show: Deep Dive: Exploring Organized Crime (Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime)
podcasts.title: Cabo Delgado: Africa's Forgotten Insurgency
podcasts.guest: Adriano Nuvunga, Zenaida Machado and Alastair Nelson
podcasts.why: Revisits the March 2021 Palma attack and the insurgency's links to illicit flows. The page shows no date or length.

media.title: Escaping Cabo Delgado's Nightmare
media.creator: Voice of America
media.where: voaafrica.com, with embed and download options.
media.why: VOA reporters visit displacement camps in Cabo Delgado. VOA is US government funded.

media.title: Orphaned and traumatized: Mozambican families fleeing ISIS struggle to rebuild their lives
media.creator: PBS NewsHour (special correspondent Neha Wadekar)
media.where: pbs.org. A broadcast news segment, not a feature film.
media.why: Covers the Palma attack, crowded displacement centres in Metuge and the arrival of boats at Ibo and Pemba.

factchecks.claim: The EU election observation mission backed Venâncio Mondlane as the winner of the 2024 election.
factchecks.by: A YouTube video of about eight minutes, denounced by MISA Mozambique in October 2024
factchecks.evidence: MISA's fact-checking unit found that the video used genuine clips of the EU mission head Laura Ballarin's press conference but that she never endorsed Mondlane's victory. Ballarin said EU missions do not declare winners or legitimise results. Mondlane had declared himself the winner, and no observer group recognised him as such. The report comes from AIM, the state news agency.

sources.title: MISA denounces video falsifying EU observer statement

factchecks.claim: Rwanda has about 4,000 to 5,000 troops in Mozambique.
factchecks.by: ISS authors (March and April 2026); the Rwandan government disputes it

factchecks.claim: Security in Cabo Delgado has improved enough for the gas project to resume safely.
factchecks.by: President Daniel Chapo, 3 February 2026 (reported by AIM)
factchecks.evidence: Chapo cited the 29 January restart as proof of improved security. ACLED's June and August updates record continued ISM kidnappings, ambushes and movement into new districts, OCHA counted more incidents in the first half of 2026 than a year earlier, and the UN rapporteur said attacks on civilians had grown. ISS says the security apparatus around the Afungi site makes a direct attack there unlikely, so the claim is stronger for the site than for the province.

local_md:
Club of Mozambique relays the OCHA count of more than 400 incidents in six months, and the state news agency AIM reports the president's claim of significant advances. [13][16]

Club of Mozambique carried the government's November 2025 statement that the audit had no deadline and that TotalEnergies could resume once it submitted a schedule within 30 days. [25]

Club of Mozambique, relaying Lusa, reports the indictment, the defence challenge and the judge's rebuke in detail. [1]

Zitamar News co-published the June investigation, and Carta's reporting on Chissale reached readers through Club of Mozambique. [2][31]

Club of Mozambique relays OCHA's funding, flood and cholera figures. [13]

AIM, the state agency, reports the Finance Ministry's timetable for an IMF agreement and the early repayment of IMF debt. [39]
international_md:
Africanews reports the UN rapporteur's finding that attacks on civilians have grown and that military victory is not in sight. [17]

The Rwandan government's own statement and the UN rapporteur's report are the main public accounts opened for this draft. [19][17]

Reuters reported the January relaunch and the open cost talks, and Oilprice, citing Bloomberg, reports the Bayphase finding. [5][20]

Al Jazeera and AP both report the charges but differ on the toll, with Amnesty cited for more than 300 dead and civil society groups for at least 400. [3][4]

CPJ and Forbidden Stories document the Valoi prosecution and the blackout, and HRW's annual report records the detentions of journalists in Macomia. [32][30][24]

RTP, using Lusa copy, reports the IOM displacement counts by province. [35]

Reuters and Oilprice report the state's projected gas revenues, and the IMF's own releases carry the debt and growth figures. [5][21][37]
scholar_md:
ACLED finds ISM spreading south and west while keeping a coastal base, and Bofin argues that military means alone will struggle to undo its coastal strategy. [6][15]

ISS says Mozambique's forces cannot secure the territory alone, that the EU faces a dilemma over funding a force whose government is accused of a role in the DRC conflict, and that Rwanda's warning may be a pressure tactic. [7]

ISS says the project resumed before the audit concluded or was published, and warns that the enclave could feed local resentment that insurgents might use for recruitment. [9]

Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera in September described the case as a judicialisation of politics and said a conviction could bar Mondlane from the 2029 race, a point ISS made in 2025. [11]

Hanlon's newsletter summarises the Forbidden Stories findings and cites HRW on the absence of credible investigations into the killings of critics. [33]

ISS warns that the economic benefits of the LNG restart for Cabo Delgado are far from guaranteed and urges transparent revenue management. [9]
